newsitem.title: UK: UK credit data reinforce case for prompt rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK credit data reinforce case for prompt rate rise.

text.p: UK consumers took on over a billion pounds of new debt in November to finance their pre-Christmas spending spree, reinforcing the case for a prompt rise in interest rates, analysts said on Friday.
Data from the Bank of England showed net consumer credit rose 1.105 billion sterling in November, with a hefty 339 million sterling increase in credit card debt.
"These numbers are very much in line with a strong consumer sector going into the new year. They reinforce the need for a further hike in rates," said Bank America analyst Jeremy Hawkins.
Consumer credit has risen by over one billion sterling in four of the last six months as consumer confidence has grown and cheap credit deals crowd the high street.

"The data shows consumer sentiment is improving," said HSBC Markets economist Dharshini David. "The amount of zero percent high street deals around, despite rising consumer demand, shows that retailers are still facing strong competition."
Hawkins said the government's 2.5 percent inflation target would look increasingly unattainable if the chunky credit numbers of recent months persisted.
"If we continue to see gains of a billion plus each month it starts to smack of a recovery in the consumer sector far too strong for an inflation target of 2.5 percent," he said.
The UK Treasury was quick to welcome the data as confirmation of growing confidence in the UK economy.
"At a personal level borrowing remains sensible and (people are) well within their ability to service the credit they want," Treasury financial secretary Michael Jack said.
Economists said the data would add to the pressure on Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to raise interest rates before the general election, which must be held by May.

"I don't think we need more evidence, but certainly at the margin, this will increase calls for a rate rise," said Deutsche Morgan Grenfell economist Ciaran Barr. He added he expected a rate rise in either January or February.
Economists are split over the likelihood of a rise in rates from their present 6.0 pct at the next monetary policy meeting between Clarke and Bank of England governor Eddie George.
But most agree the Chancellor will have to bite the bullet and raise rates before the country goes to the polls.
Hawkins said November's credit data was consistent with the government's budget forecast of a 4.25 percent rise in domestic consumer expenditure in 1997.

"The figures bode well for a strong recovery in the consumer sector. It may prove that the government got the real economy side right (in the budget forecast) but if that is the case, it's not compatible with existing interest rates," he said.
